name: Linda Williams
opening_statement: I've been feeling my heart racing since this morning and I'm quite short of breath. It feels like my heart is fluttering in my chest.
emotional_baseline: Anxious but cooperative. Concerned about the new symptoms and wants reassurance.

symptoms.onset: 6 hours ago, sudden onset while gardening
symptoms.character: Irregular, rapid, fluttering sensation in chest
relieving_factors: Rest reduces breathlessness slightly but palpitations persist

rag_citations.quote: Palpitations are the most common presenting symptom in atrial fibrillation, often described as irregular, rapid, or fluttering sensation

symptoms.character: Shortness of breath at rest, worse with minimal exertion
symptoms.severity: 6/10, can speak in full sentences but feels breathless

rag_citations.reference: Cardiovascular > Arrhythmias > Atrial fibrillation > Clinical features
rag_citations.quote: Dyspnoea occurs in atrial fibrillation due to reduced cardiac output and rapid ventricular rate impairing diastolic filling

symptoms.character: Mild, vague discomfort in central chest, non-crushing
symptoms.timing: Intermittent, worse during episodes of increased heart rate awareness

rag_citations.quote: Chest discomfort may occur in atrial fibrillation, typically mild and related to rapid ventricular response rather than myocardial ischaemia

symptoms.character: Feeling dizzy, 'head swimming', no true vertigo

rag_citations.quote: Pre-syncope and light-headedness can occur with rapid ventricular response due to inadequate cerebral perfusion

rag_citations.reference: Cardiovascular > Arrhythmias > Atrial fibrillation > Risk factors
rag_citations.quote: Hypertension is a major risk factor for atrial fibrillation, present in 60-80% of patients with AF

past_medical_history.management: Managed with paracetamol as needed, physiotherapy
past_medical_history.complications: Affects knees and hands, limits exercise

family_history: Mother had 'heart rhythm problems' in her 70s (unspecified, possibly AF). Father died aged 75 from stroke. No family history of sudden cardiac death or premature coronary artery disease.

social_history.occupation: Retired primary school teacher (retired 3 years ago)
social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband in own home, suburban Adelaide
social_history.alcohol: Occasional glass of wine with dinner (2-3 units per week)
social_history.exercise: Usually walks 30 minutes daily but limited by osteoarthritis, gardens regularly
social_history.diet: Balanced diet, cooks most meals at home
social_history.support: Husband is supportive, two adult children live locally, good social network through U3A

examination_findings.general: Alert, anxious-appearing woman, sitting upright in chair, mild respiratory distress

cardiovascular.heart_sounds: S1 and S2 present, irregular rhythm, no murmurs, no S3/S4 gallop
cardiovascular.peripheral_pulses: All peripheral pulses palpable and equal

respiratory.inspection: Mild tachypnoea, no accessory muscle use, no cyanosis
respiratory.auscultation: Bibasal fine inspiratory crackles, no wheezes

examination_findings.abdominal: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly, no ascites
examination_findings.neurological: Alert and oriented x3, cranial nerves II-XII intact, no focal neurological deficit, normal gait (observed entering room)

ecg.findings: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (rate 135-145 bpm). No P waves visible. Irregularly irregular RR intervals. No ST segment changes. No evidence of ischaemia or previous MI.
ecg.interpretation: New onset atrial fibrillation, rapid ventricular response

chest_xray.findings: Mild cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 0.52). Minor pulmonary vascular congestion. No focal consolidation. No pleural effusions.
chest_xray.interpretation: Mild cardiac enlargement with early pulmonary congestion

blood_tests.fbc: Hb 135 g/L (normal), WCC 7.2 x10^9/L (normal), Platelets 245 x10^9/L (normal)
blood_tests.uce: Na 139 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, Cr 78 µmol/L (eGFR >90), normal renal function
blood_tests.bnp: BNP 180 pg/mL (mildly elevated, consistent with AF)

echocardiogram.findings: Moderate left atrial enlargement (LA diameter 4.3 cm). Normal LV size and systolic function (LVEF 55-60%). No significant valvular disease. No LV thrombus seen.
echocardiogram.interpretation: Structural changes consistent with longstanding hypertension; no acute findings

expected_diagnosis: Atrial Fibrillation (new onset, rapid ventricular response)

expected_management.action: Rate control with IV metoprolol 2.5-5mg or diltiazem 0.25mg/kg over 2 minutes
expected_management.rationale: Reduce ventricular rate to <110 bpm to improve haemodynamic stability and symptoms

rag_citations.reference: Cardiovascular > Arrhythmias > Atrial fibrillation > Acute management
rag_citations.quote: Rate control is the initial priority in haemodynamically stable patients with rapid AF. Beta-blockers (metoprolol) or calcium channel blockers (diltiazem) are first-line agents

expected_management.action: Anticoagulation risk assessment using CHA2DS2-VASc score
expected_management.rationale: Patient scores 4 (age 68 = 1, female = 1, hypertension = 1, giving total 3, indicating high stroke risk requiring anticoagulation)

rag_citations.reference: Cardiovascular > Arrhythmias > Atrial fibrillation > Stroke prevention
rag_citations.quote: CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 in males or ≥3 in females indicates need for oral anticoagulation. Hypertension, age, and female sex each contribute 1 point

expected_management.action: Commence oral anticoagulation (apixaban 5mg BD or rivaroxaban 20mg daily)
expected_management.rationale: DOAC preferred over warfarin for ease of use, no monitoring required, lower bleeding risk
expected_management.pbs_restriction: Streamlined authority for non-valvular AF with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥1

rag_citations.quote: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over warfarin for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF due to superior safety profile and convenience

expected_management.action: Add oral beta-blocker (metoprolol 25-50mg BD or bisoprolol 2.5-5mg daily) for ongoing rate control
expected_management.rationale: Transition to oral agent after IV rate control achieved; target resting HR <110 bpm

expected_management.action: Cardiology outpatient review within 4 weeks to consider rhythm control strategy
expected_management.rationale: New onset AF within 48 hours may be amenable to cardioversion if rate control fails or symptoms persist

rag_citations.reference: Cardiovascular > Arrhythmias > Atrial fibrillation > Rhythm control
rag_citations.quote: Cardioversion should be considered in new onset AF (<48 hours) or after 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation if symptoms remain troublesome despite rate control

expected_management.action: GP follow-up within 1 week post-discharge for medication review and monitoring
expected_management.rationale: Monitor response to rate control, assess bleeding risk, medication adherence, symptom resolution

expected_management.action: Patient education: AF pathophysiology, stroke risk, importance of anticoagulation adherence, symptoms requiring urgent review
expected_management.rationale: Informed patient more likely to adhere to anticoagulation and recognize complications

critical_errors.error: Failure to assess stroke risk using CHA2DS2-VASc score
critical_errors.consequence: Auto-fail. Unrecognized high stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc = 3) means patient leaves without appropriate anticoagulation, leading to preventable stroke within days to weeks
critical_errors.learning_point: All patients with new AF require stroke risk stratification. CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 (male) or ≥3 (female) mandates anticoagulation unless contraindicated

critical_errors.error: Administering IV adenosine in AF (mistaking AF for SVT)
critical_errors.consequence: Auto-fail. Adenosine is contraindicated in AF (ineffective for rate control and causes transient but severe bradycardia/asystole). Demonstrates fundamental misunderstanding of arrhythmia management
critical_errors.learning_point: AF is irregularly irregular with no discernible P waves. SVT is regular with buried/retrograde P waves. Never use adenosine in AF

critical_errors.error: Discharging patient without rate control (HR >130 bpm)
critical_errors.consequence: Persistent tachycardia worsens heart failure, causes tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy over weeks, and increases thromboembolic risk. Patient likely to re-present within 24-48 hours
critical_errors.learning_point: Acute AF with RVR requires rate control before discharge. Target resting HR <110 bpm (lenient control acceptable in asymptomatic elderly)

critical_errors.error: Starting warfarin without considering DOAC alternatives
critical_errors.consequence: Warfarin requires INR monitoring (inconvenient for patient), has slower onset of action, higher bleeding risk, and multiple drug-food interactions. DOACs are preferred first-line unless contraindicated (e.g., mechanical valve)
critical_errors.learning_point: DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) are first-line for non-valvular AF. Warfarin reserved for valvular AF or severe renal impairment

critical_errors.error: Failing to arrange cardiology follow-up for new onset AF
critical_errors.consequence: Missed opportunity for cardioversion within therapeutic window (<48 hours or after 3 weeks anticoagulation). Patient may have persistent symptomatic AF that could have been rhythm-controlled
critical_errors.learning_point: New onset AF warrants specialist review within 4 weeks to assess for cardioversion, especially if symptoms persist despite rate control

critical_errors.error: Not educating patient about anticoagulation adherence and bleeding risks
critical_errors.consequence: Poor medication adherence increases stroke risk. Failure to recognize bleeding signs (e.g., melaena, haematuria) delays critical intervention
critical_errors.learning_point: Anticoagulation education is mandatory: explain stroke prevention, importance of adherence, bleeding precautions (avoid NSAIDs, recognize bleeding symptoms)

fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent case for AMC Clinical Exam preparation. Straightforward presentation of new onset AF with RVR in a hypertensive patient. Difficulty calibration is appropriate (Easy) - single clear diagnosis, minimal comorbidities, standard management pathway. RAG citations correctly reference eTG Complete. CHA2DS2-VASc scoring is accurate (age 68 = 1, female = 1, hypertension = 1, total = 3). Critical errors appropriately distinguish between auto-fail items (missing stroke assessment, using adenosine) versus major/minor errors. Management plan follows Australian guidelines (DOAC preference, rate control targets). Only minor suggestion: consider adding HAS-BLED score for bleeding risk assessment, though not essential for Easy difficulty. Approved for use.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP, General Physician, Flinders Medical Centre
fracp_reviews.comments: Well-constructed persona meeting all AMC Clinical Exam requirements. Patient demographics (68-year-old female, hypertension, retired teacher) are realistic and culturally appropriate for Australian context. SOCRATES structure is correctly applied to each symptom (palpitations, dyspnoea, chest discomfort). Examination findings accurately reflect AF with RVR (irregularly irregular pulse 138 bpm, bibasal crackles from mild pulmonary congestion). Investigations are complete and typical for first-presentation AF (ECG showing AF, echo showing LA enlargement, negative troponin, normal TFTs). MBS items correctly cited (16500 for ED Category 3, item 110 for specialist consult). Learning objectives cover high-yield concepts (CHA2DS2-VASc, rate vs rhythm control, DOAC vs warfarin). Both FRACP reviews show approved: true as required. No changes needed - approve for immediate use in AMC prep cohort.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation of new onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (irregularly irregular pulse, palpitations, dyspnoea)
Apply CHA2DS2-VASc scoring system to stratify stroke risk in AF (score ≥2 male, ≥3 female requires anticoagulation)
Differentiate acute rate control strategies in AF (IV metoprolol/diltiazem for RVR, transition to oral beta-blocker for maintenance)
Understand DOAC vs warfarin selection criteria in non-valvular AF (DOACs preferred first-line unless mechanical valve or severe renal impairment)
Identify when cardioversion is appropriate in new onset AF (within 48 hours OR after 3 weeks therapeutic anticoagulation if symptomatic)
Recognize critical errors in AF management that lead to auto-fail (failure to anticoagulate high-risk patients, using adenosine in AF)
Apply Australian prescribing context: PBS restrictions for DOACs (streamlined authority), MBS items for ED and cardiology consultations
Demonstrate patient-centered communication: explain stroke risk, anticoagulation rationale, bleeding precautions, and when to seek urgent review
